items.text: A "science centre career" in India is not one job.
The single biggest organisation to know is NCSM.
Notice how different these roles are from each other.

blocks.heading: NCSM Does Not Run One Central Annual

items.text: Honest take: this is genuinely multi-stage competition

blocks.heading: What AI Is Actually Changing Here

items.text: AI tools are already changing the content-production side of this field, not the physical or curatorial judgment side.

What AI is not doing here is replacing the human judgment that makes a science centre role valuable: deciding what is scientifically accurate and age-appropriate, reading a live audience during a demonstration, and building the trust that makes a school group actually listen.

A real, growing number of people who care about explaining science to the public in India build that career without ever joining a science museum: through YouTube channels, science writing, illustrated explainers, live workshops for schools, and consulting work for research institutes, edtech companies, or science-outreach nonprofits that need someone who can make complex ideas simple.
Institutional roles pay a modest but real, guaranteed salary from day one.

Many working science communicators in India run both at once: a stable job (inside or outside a science centre) alongside a slowly growing independent audience, only stepping fully into independent work once that audience and its income are already proven.
It is closer to seven separate roles (curator, exhibit developer, education officer, technical assistant, planetarium educator, administration, and outreach/content) inside one organisation.
NCSM runs 25-odd centres nationwide and released well under 100 posts across its 2025-2026 recruitment cycles, spread across curator, technical, and support grades.
A government written/aptitude test is only the first filter.
